This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), fever and pain due to a cold, low back pain, dysmenorrhea, post-operative pain and ankylosing spondylitis, headache, toothache, muscle pain, neuralgia, acute gout, psoriatic arthritis, soft tissue injury (sprain, contusion), and non-articular rheumatic diseases (tendinitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis).

At a glance

Category

OTC medicine

Why this one

Products sharing general-name code 172806ATB have the same ingredient, strength and form — check by ingredient, not by brand name.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 1/2 to 1.5 tablets (200 to 600 mg) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and may take up to a maximum of 3200 mg per day. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30-40 mg per kg of body weight per day in 3 to 4 divided doses; for mild to moderate pain or a cold, adults take 1/2 to 1 tablet (200 to 400 mg) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Children aged 11 to 14 take 200 to 250 mg per dose, those aged 7 to 10 take 150 to 200 mg per dose, those aged 3 to 6 take 100 to 150 mg per dose, and those aged 1 to 2 take 50 to 100 mg per dose, orally 3 to 4 times a day. For children weighing less than 30 kg, the daily amount should not exceed 500 mg, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. Do not take more than the recommended dose.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine; patients with or with a history of gastrointestinal ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood disorders, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe hypertension, or bronchial asthma; patients with or with a history of hypersensitivity such as asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (including COX-2 inhibitors); patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery (heart artery) bypass surgery; pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy; patients taking high-dose methotrexate as anticancer therapy; and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with or with a history of blood disorders, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis or with or with a history of hepatic impairment, patients with or with a history of renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency or heart disease, hypertension, systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, the elderly and children, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and patients hypersensitive to Yellow No. 5 should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, or serious and potentially fatal gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation (puncture) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If any of the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: shock symptoms (chest burning, chills, difficulty breathing, decreased blood pressure); blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), and eosinophilia; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation (puncture), ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, hematemesis, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, oral ulcers, constipation, black stools; mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reactions, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome), angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, skin reddening, blisters, rash; hepatic dysfunction such as hepatitis, jaundice, and elevation of GOT, GPT, and ALP, hepatic impairment, hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reactions, asthma attacks, urticaria, eczema, purpura (purple spots), rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, difficulty breathing or wheezing; visual disturbances such as areas of visual loss, hearing loss (deafness), tinnitus, taste disturbance, dizziness, drowsiness, lightheadedness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (symptoms such as severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness); increased blood pressure, palpitations (throbbing), heart failure, myocardial infarction or angina; acute renal failure, oliguria (decreased urine), hematuria, proteinuria, elevation of BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and accompanying shortness of breath, lethargy, swelling around the eyes, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed, and peripheral edema.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, low-dose aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • When taken together with ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used for allergic rhinitis (sneezing, nasal congestion, itching, a burning sensation in the eyes) and chronic idiopathic (of unknown cause) urticaria.

At a glance

Category

OTC medicine

Why this one

Products sharing general-name code 185401ATB have the same ingredient, strength and form — check by ingredient, not by brand name.

How to take it

Adults and children aged 12 years or older take 1 tablet (10 mg) once a day. Children aged 6 to under 12 years take 1 tablet (10 mg) once a day if they weigh 30 kg or more, and 1/2 tablet (5 mg) once a day if they weigh 30 kg or less. The dose may be adjusted appropriately according to age and symptoms.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, children under 6 years of age, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with hepatic impairment or renal failure should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If sedation, anticholinergic effects, headache, fainting, drowsiness, thirst, gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, gastritis), increased appetite, tachycardia, fatigue, rash, alopecia, anaphylaxis including angioedema, hepatic dysfunction, supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, palpitations, dizziness, or convulsions occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take it together with cimetidine, erythromycin, ketoconazole, quinidine, fluconazole, fluoxetine, or drugs that inhibit hepatic metabolism.

At a glance

Category

Why this one

Products sharing general-name code 136603ATB have the same ingredient, strength and form — check by ingredient, not by brand name.

How to take it

Adults take 1/2 to 1 tablet (125 to 250 mg) per dose, 3 times a day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with peptic ulcer, patients in whom drug-induced disturbance (restlessness) of the stomach or duodenum has occurred, patients hypersensitive to this drug, those who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or an allergic reaction to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors), patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, pregnant women, and patients with severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe heart failure, or inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis must not take this drug.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with a history of peptic ulcer, children and the elderly, patients with hypertension, fluid retention (fluid accumulation) or heart failure, or bronchial asthma, those with hepatic impairment or a history thereof, those with renal impairment or a history thereof, and lactating women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain (stomachache), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer and perforation (a hole), rarely shock, rash, itching, anemia, elevation of AST and ALT, drowsiness, headache, dizziness, cold sweats, chills, abnormal euphoria, or the like appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor antagonists, aspirin, diuretics, lithium, methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin, etc.), cyclosporine and tacrolimus, antiplatelet agents and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), or corticosteroids together.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients who are also being treated for peptic ulcer with misoprostol or a similar agent should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Before taking this medicine, patients taking antibiotics such as erythromycin, cephalexin, cefuroxime, amoxicillin, doxycycline, and oxytetracycline should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used for seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, chronic idiopathic urticaria, and pruritus, and for eczema and dermatitis when used together with a topical hydrocortisone preparation.

At a glance

Category

OTC medicine

Why this one

Products sharing general-name code 130501ATB have the same ingredient, strength and form — check by ingredient, not by brand name.

How to take it

Adults and children aged 6 years or older take 1 tablet (10 mg) once a day before bedtime; patients sensitive to adverse reactions take 1/2 tablet (5 mg) each in the morning and evening in divided doses. The dose may be adjusted appropriately according to age and symptoms. The dosing interval for patients with moderate to severe (severe symptoms) renal impairment should be adjusted according to the patient's renal function, and for pediatric patients with renal impairment the dose should be individually adjusted taking into account the patient's renal clearance and body weight, so refer to the approved labeling information for details.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine or to hydroxyzine or piperazine derivatives, patients with renal failure, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, infants under 6 years of age, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with renal impairment or hepatic impairment, the elderly, patients with epilepsy and patients at risk of seizures, and patients with predisposing factors for urinary retention (spinal cord lesions, prostatic hyperplasia, etc.) should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If drowsiness, headache, occasionally malaise, numbness, asthenia, agitation, paresthesia, rarely mild and transient languor, fatigue, dizziness, heavy-headedness, excitement, convulsions, dyskinesia, dystonia, syncope, tremor, aggression, confusion, depression, hallucinations, insomnia, tic disorder, amnesia, memory impairment, suicidal ideation, nightmares, occasionally thirst, dry lips, nausea, loss of appetite, epigastric discomfort, indigestion, abdominal pain, stomach pain, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, rarely vomiting, gastrointestinal disorder, cheilitis, taste abnormality, increased appetite, rarely tachycardia, arrhythmia, elevated blood pressure, occasionally palpitations, vasculitis, occasionally leukopenia, neutropenia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia, rarely monocytosis, increased or decreased platelets, photosensitivity, rarely hypersensitivity and anaphylactic shock, urticaria, angioedema, fixed drug eruption, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, rarely blurred vision, conjunctival hyperemia, accommodation disorder, oculogyration, vertigo, occasionally elevated BUN, glycosuria, blood in urine, rarely difficulty urinating, nocturnal enuresis, joint pain, urinary retention, pharyngitis, cough, nosebleed, bronchospasm, hearing abnormality, visual abnormality, occasionally chest pain, rarely menstrual irregularity, tinnitus, rhinitis, or weight gain occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • After stopping this medicine, itching, urticaria, and similar reactions may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with theophylline, ritonavir, or excessive alcohol while taking it.

This medicine is used for nutritional supplementation in cases of nourishment and tonic effects, weak constitution, physical fatigue, febrile/wasting diseases during or after illness (during the course of an illness or after recovery), pregnancy/lactation, etc.

At a glance

Category

OTC medicine

Why this one

Products sharing general-name code C36200ACH have the same ingredient, strength and form — check by ingredient, not by brand name.

How to take it

Children aged 15 years or older and adults take 2 capsules per dose, 1 to 2 times a day.

Warning

  • Taking 5,000 IU or more of vitamin A a day may cause congenital malformations.
  • Women within the first 3 months of pregnancy or who may be pregnant should not take this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this drug, infants under 3 months of age, and patients with hypercalcemia (a condition in which calcium is present in excess in the blood), sarcoidosis, or renal disease must not take this drug.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants under 12 months of age, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and lactating women, patients with hyperoxaluria (a condition in which excessive amounts of oxalate are excreted in the urine), patients with a thrombotic (blood vessel blockage) predisposition, and patients deficient in folic acid should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • It may interfere with the detection of glucose in various urine tests, and may turn the urine yellow, affecting clinical test values.

Possible side effects

  • If nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, itching, dry and rough skin, painful joint swelling, loose stools, gastric distension, abdominal discomfort, constipation, rash, redness (congested and reddened), loss of appetite, or menstruation coming earlier than scheduled or the amount gradually increasing and bleeding lasting for a long time appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with levodopa.
  • When taken together with estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
